about: The second silence of the Canon. Cum signo fídei — with the sign of faith — has meant baptism since antiquity: the prayer remembers the baptized. Dórmiunt in somno pacis speaks of the dead in the language of the catacombs, where in pace was the commonest epitaph and refrigérium — a cooling — the ordinary word for what was asked for them. The petition holds off to the very end: locum waits six words for its verb.

s01.translation: Be mindful also, O Lord, of thy servants and handmaids who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep the sleep of peace.

s02.narrative: The priest joins his hands and prays a while in silence for those dead he means to remember; then he spreads his hands and goes on.

s03.translation: To them, O Lord, and to all who rest in Christ, we plead that thou grant a place of refreshment, of light and of peace.

s04.narrative: The priest joins his hands and bows his head.

s05.translation: Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

w001.function: A future imperative, as in the commemoration of the living.

w002.function: One word divides this prayer from its twin before the consecration.

w006.function: Here the missal prints N. et N. and the priest falls silent. This edition does not print the blank, so the relative clause that follows describes the servants and handmaids themselves.

w011.function: Signum fídei has meant baptism since antiquity.

w014.function: A present beside a perfect: they went before us once, and they are sleeping now.

w018.function: A dative with “indúlgeas” (w031): to whom the grant is to be made.

w024.function: A participle used as a noun: those resting in Christ.

w025.function: The object of “indúlgeas” (w031), six words away; Latin keeps the verb to the very end of the clause.

w026.function: Literally a cooling; in early Christian epitaphs the ordinary word for what was asked for the dead.

w032.function: A deponent; it stands after the clause it governs, the reverse of the English order.
